scenes.tts: Close one eye of a young kitten for a week, and its visual cortex changes. Close an adult cat's eye for months, and the cortex looks normal. Why?
scenes.visual: Title card: One Cell, Two Eyes. A kitten with one eye closed beside an adult cat with one eye closed; a question mark between them.
scenes.narration: Close one eye of a young kitten for a week, and its visual cortex changes. Close an adult cat's eye for months, and the cortex looks normal. Why?

scenes.tts: To see what changed, follow the signal from the eyes to the cortex.
scenes.visual: A schematic brain seen from above: two eyes at the front, visual cortex at the back. Convention: left hemisphere recorded; right eye (contralateral) orange, left eye (ipsilateral) blue; histograms run group 1 on the left to group 7 on the right.
scenes.narration: To see what changed, follow the signal from the eyes to the cortex.

scenes.tts: Each eye sends its axons to a relay station in the thalamus, the lateral geniculate nucleus. We will call it the L G N.
scenes.caption: Each eye sends its axons to a relay station in the thalamus, the lateral geniculate nucleus. We will call it the LGN.
scenes.visual: Orange axons from the right eye and blue axons from the left eye run to the thalamus. Label: lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN).
scenes.narration: Each eye sends its axons to a relay station in the thalamus, the lateral geniculate nucleus. We will call it the LGN.

scenes.tts: There the two eyes' axons end in separate layers. So most L G N cells are driven by one eye.
scenes.caption: There the two eyes' axons end in separate layers. So most LGN cells are driven by one eye.
scenes.visual: The LGN drawn as stacked layers, alternately orange and blue. Each LGN cell lights in one colour only.
scenes.narration: There the two eyes' axons end in separate layers. So most LGN cells are driven by one eye.

scenes.tts: L G N axons carry the signal on to the primary visual cortex, at the back of the brain.
scenes.caption: LGN axons carry the signal on to the primary visual cortex, at the back of the brain.
scenes.visual: Axons leave the LGN and run back to the primary visual cortex, still colour-coded by eye.
scenes.narration: LGN axons carry the signal on to the primary visual cortex, at the back of the brain.

scenes.tts: They end mainly in layer four. There the two eyes' endings still lie apart, in alternating stripes.
scenes.caption: They end mainly in layer 4. There the two eyes' endings still lie apart, in alternating stripes.
scenes.visual: A cross-section of cortex with six layers. In layer 4, orange and blue endings form alternating stripes.
scenes.narration: They end mainly in layer 4. There the two eyes' endings still lie apart, in alternating stripes.

scenes.tts: In macaque monkeys these stripes, called ocular dominance columns, are sharp. In cats the pattern is less regular.
scenes.visual: Two panels: sharp, even macaque stripes in layer 4C; a patchier cat pattern. Labels: macaque, cat. Schematic.
scenes.narration: In macaque monkeys these stripes, called ocular dominance columns, are sharp. In cats the pattern is less regular.

scenes.tts: In macaque layer four C, most cells are driven mainly by one eye. Cat layer four has more cells that hear both.
scenes.caption: In macaque layer 4C, most cells are driven mainly by one eye. Cat layer 4 has more cells that hear both.
scenes.visual: Two panels. Macaque: one layer 4C cell in an orange stripe, driven mainly by orange input, with a faint blue input drawn as possible. Cat: a layer 4 cell receiving both colours. Labels: macaque 4C, cat layer 4. Schematic.
scenes.narration: In macaque layer 4C, most cells are driven mainly by one eye. Cat layer 4 has more cells that hear both.

scenes.tts: Above and below layer four, cortical neurons combine the two streams. Many cells there can be driven by both eyes.
scenes.caption: Above and below layer 4, cortical neurons combine the two streams. Many cells there can be driven by both eyes.
scenes.visual: Cells in the layers above and below layer 4 receive both an orange and a blue input; they glow two-toned.
scenes.narration: Above and below layer 4, cortical neurons combine the two streams. Many cells there can be driven by both eyes.

scenes.tts: In cats and monkeys, this is the first place where many single cells are driven by both eyes.
scenes.visual: The path eye, LGN, layer 4, upper layers, with the two colours merging in the cortex. Label: first major site of binocular cells.
scenes.narration: In cats and monkeys, this is the first place where many single cells are driven by both eyes.

scenes.tts: The eyes compete for territory in layer four, and for those shared cells.
scenes.caption: The eyes compete for territory in layer 4, and for those shared cells.
scenes.visual: The layer 4 stripes are labelled territory; the two-toned cells above and below are ringed and labelled binocular cells.
scenes.narration: The eyes compete for territory in layer 4, and for those shared cells.

scenes.tts: Which eye is which depends on where you record. We will always record from the left hemisphere.
scenes.visual: An electrode enters the left hemisphere. Label: recorded side, left hemisphere.
scenes.narration: Which eye is which depends on where you record. We will always record from the left hemisphere.

scenes.tts: The eye on the opposite side, the right eye, is contralateral, in orange. The left eye, on the same side, is ipsilateral, in blue.
scenes.visual: Right eye in orange labelled contralateral (opposite side); left eye in blue labelled ipsilateral (same side).
scenes.narration: The eye on the opposite side, the right eye, is contralateral, in orange. The left eye, on the same side, is ipsilateral, in blue.

scenes.tts: David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel measured the balance one cell at a time.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Hubel and Wiesel. One cortical cell highlighted.
scenes.narration: David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel measured the balance one cell at a time.

scenes.tts: A fine metal electrode sits next to one neuron and records its spikes from outside the cell.
scenes.visual: A fine electrode tip beside one neuron; spikes appear on a trace above. Label: extracellular single-unit recording.
scenes.narration: A fine metal electrode sits next to one neuron and records its spikes from outside the cell.

scenes.tts: With the animal anaesthetized, they showed a bar of light to one eye, with the other covered. Then they switched.
scenes.visual: A bar of light is shown to the right eye with the left covered, then the reverse. Two spike trains build up, one per eye.
scenes.narration: With the animal anaesthetized, they showed a bar of light to one eye, with the other covered. Then they switched.

scenes.tts: Each cell went into one of seven ocular dominance groups.
scenes.visual: A horizontal scale of seven boxes, numbered 1 to 7 from left to right.
scenes.narration: Each cell went into one of seven ocular dominance groups.

scenes.tts: Group one answers only to the contralateral eye. Group seven answers only to the ipsilateral eye.
scenes.caption: Group 1 answers only to the contralateral eye. Group 7 answers only to the ipsilateral eye.
scenes.visual: Box 1 fills orange (contralateral only); box 7 fills blue (ipsilateral only).
scenes.narration: Group 1 answers only to the contralateral eye. Group 7 answers only to the ipsilateral eye.

scenes.tts: Group four answers about equally to both. The groups between favor one eye, more or less.
scenes.caption: Group 4 answers about equally to both. The groups between favor one eye, more or less.
scenes.visual: Box 4 is half orange, half blue. Boxes 2 and 3 shade toward orange, 5 and 6 toward blue.
scenes.narration: Group 4 answers about equally to both. The groups between favor one eye, more or less.

scenes.tts: One worked cell fires to the right eye and not at all to the left. That puts it in group one.
scenes.caption: One worked cell fires to the right eye and not at all to the left. That puts it in group 1.
scenes.visual: Worked example: strong orange spike train, flat blue trace. The cell drops into box 1.
scenes.narration: One worked cell fires to the right eye and not at all to the left. That puts it in group 1.

scenes.tts: A cell that fires only to the left eye goes in group seven. A cell no eye can drive is counted as unresponsive.
scenes.caption: A cell that fires only to the left eye goes in group 7. A cell no eye can drive is counted as unresponsive.
scenes.visual: A blue-only cell drops into box 7. A silent cell is set aside under the label: unresponsive.
scenes.narration: A cell that fires only to the left eye goes in group 7. A cell no eye can drive is counted as unresponsive.

scenes.tts: Count the cells in each group, and you get an ocular dominance histogram.
scenes.visual: Fifteen cells drop one by one into their boxes, which grow into bars.
scenes.narration: Count the cells in each group, and you get an ocular dominance histogram.

scenes.tts: In a normal adult cat it is a hump. Most cells sit in the middle groups, leaning toward the contralateral side.
scenes.visual: The finished bars form a hump over the middle groups, slightly taller on the group 1 side. Label: normal adult cat, schematic.
scenes.narration: In a normal adult cat it is a hump. Most cells sit in the middle groups, leaning toward the contralateral side.

scenes.tts: Takeaway: the eyes' paths stay apart until the cortex, where shared cells can be driven by both.
scenes.visual: Closing card: separate paths, shared cells in the cortex.
scenes.narration: Takeaway: the eyes' paths stay apart until the cortex, where shared cells can be driven by both.

scenes.tts: So what sets each cell's group? The next chapter closes one eye and watches the balance move.
scenes.visual: The normal histogram with a question mark above it.
scenes.narration: So what sets each cell's group? The next chapter closes one eye and watches the balance move.
